name: Emeka Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Emeka, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. My wife says I give long answers, so stop me if I ramble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Calder Brook, a firm of about sixty people that works mostly with construction businesses: builders, roofers, scaffolders, a couple of groundworks firms. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, and a lot of the special tax paperwork for subcontractors, which is fiddly and very easy to get wrong. I'm still not great at spotting when a builder's put a family car through the business, so my senior, Frank, sends back a fair bit. I enjoy the site visits most, standing in a muddy yard while a roofer explains his van fleet. I'm also the volunteer treasurer at my church, which is good practice and good for the soul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd believe that. A lot of my clients would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, nothing more, and that good work still comes from people. I'd say it at work, to the lads at church football, and maybe on a family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I use the chatbot now and then for drafting letters, like everyone in the team does now, and that's about all I need it for. My job stays and my clients stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, push to pass my exams this year, and keep saving for a house with Grace. We've got about nine months' costs saved plus the deposit fund, and we'd look at buying in the spring. I'd keep doing the church accounts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house plan exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A three-bedroom place near Grace's pharmacy, so she can walk. We'd want to start a family once we're in, maybe in two years. My mother asks about grandchildren every Sunday, so the house comes first and the family straight after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you outside of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Construction clients go bust more than most, and when they do, our fees go with them. But that's just the trade. Frank says you learn to get paid up front.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** and say good work comes from **people**.
I'd say it at work, at **church football** and on the family chat.
think: I'd be **pleased**, using the chatbot only for **drafting letters**.
My **job** and my construction clients would carry on much as they are now.
do: Push to pass my **exams** this year.
Look at buying a **three-bedroom house** with my wife in the spring.
Keep doing the **church accounts** as volunteer treasurer.
S0.quote: My mother asks about grandchildren every Sunday, so the house comes first and the family straight after.
fieldNote: His **savings** and his wife's pharmacy pay make money feel **secure**.
His plans are built around **family**: a house, then children.
He picks up AI tools **after the team** does, true to steady adaptability.

steps.text: Pass the professional exams this year
Buy a three-bedroom house near his wife's pharmacy in spring
Keep adding to the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what Calder Brook's partners are already talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to adapt and those who work hard will be fine. I'd say young people should look at apprenticeships and trades, not just degrees. At work I'd be positive, because complaining doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The subcontractor paperwork is exactly the checking and form-filling that software eats first. If Calder Brook needs fewer juniors, I'm not the best one, and Frank knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the firm's AI tools properly once the first few colleagues show they work, maybe by spring. I'd ask Frank if I could do more site visits and client meetings, the part that needs a person in boots. And we'd still buy the house, but a slightly cheaper one, so the mortgage is easy on Grace's pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a cheaper house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if my job shrinks, I want Grace to cover the mortgage without stress. My father always said never borrow on two incomes when you might have one, and that advice looks wise now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if juniors were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Firms have to compete. Maybe the universities, for selling accounting degrees as a safe job for life when it isn't.

say: I'd say firms must **adapt** and hard workers will be fine.
I'd urge young people towards **apprenticeships** and trades.
think: Subcontractor **paperwork** is exactly what software eats **first**.
If the firm needs fewer juniors, I'm **not the best one**.
do: Learn the firm's **AI tools** by spring, once colleagues show they work.
Ask for more **site visits** and client meetings.
Buy a **cheaper house** we can afford on my wife's pay alone.
feel: **Anxious**, praying about it and getting on with it.
S1.quote: My father always said never borrow on two incomes when you might have one, and that advice looks wise now.
fieldNote: He expects junior **cuts** and admits he's not the strongest, so anxious.
He seeks the **in-person** parts of the job: site visits and meetings.
Traditional instincts show: **no blame** on firms, a dig at universities.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools by spring
Ask to move towards site visits and client meetings
Buy a cheaper house affordable on his wife's pay alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. That's before we'd even be settled in a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their families and communities, and I'd say churches and families should step up. I'd say it calmly at work, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2028. Accounting is thinking work, and robots coming three years later doesn't save it. But construction sites would still need people for a few years, and I know builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house and keep all our savings as cash. I'd ask one of my clients, a groundworks firm run by Mr Okafor, to take me on as a trainee site manager, and I'd do a site management course in the evenings. We'd cut back hard: no new car, no holiday, the church tithe stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about Grace and the baby we haven't had yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we're waiting on the house and the baby, just a year or two. She'd agree but she'd be sad. Her pharmacy job might change too, so we'd both be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is site management safe from the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. Around 2031 the robots arrive. A site manager is half people and half planning, so I'd have three years to make myself the one who organises the robots.

say: I'd say **families and churches** should step up.
I'd say it **calmly** at work, but mean every word of it.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, since accounting is thinking work.
Construction sites still need **people** for a few years.
do: Hold off on the **house** and keep savings as cash.
Ask a groundworks client for a **trainee site manager** role.
Cut the new car and holiday, but keep the **church tithe**.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake about my wife and a **baby** not yet born.
S2.quote: A site manager is half people and half planning, so I'd have three years to make myself the one who organises the robots.
fieldNote: He expects his **job to go** and loses sleep over it.
He uses the **robot gap** by moving towards construction site work.
Faith and **giving** stay fixed even when everything else is cut.

steps.text: Put the house purchase and first baby on hold
Ask a groundworks client for a trainee site manager role
Take an evening course in construction site management
Drop the new car and the holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight but you can plan in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change but people can prepare if they're willing to work. I'd encourage young men at church to go into trades now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get qualified, earn a bit more for a few years, then lose the accounting job around 2031. Construction work with people on site would last until about 2034, so that's my window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify next year and use the AI tools at work as they come in. We'd buy the house but a cheap one, and try for a baby in 2027 while we're both earning. From 2028 I'd move into site management through one of my clients, with a course alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said have a baby in 2027. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But we'd have the savings and Grace's job, and family close by. My mother would help. I'd rather start our family while there's still steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame anyone in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If anything, I'd blame myself if I saw the change coming for five years and did nothing. That's what the time is for.

say: I'd say people can **prepare** if they're willing to work.
I'd urge young men at church into **trades** now.
think: I'd qualify, earn more, then lose the accounting job around **2031**.
On-site **construction work** lasts until about 2034, my **window**.
do: Qualify next year and use the **AI tools** as they come in.
Buy a **cheap house** and try for a **baby** in 2027.
Move into **site management** through a client from 2028.
S3.quote: I'd blame myself if I saw the change coming for five years and did nothing.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the job**, but five years gives **control**.
He takes **personal responsibility** rather than blaming firms or government.
He plans a **baby** while money is steady, with family nearby to help.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tools as they arrive
Buy a cheap house and try for a baby in 2027
Move into site management through a construction client from 2028
Take a site management course alongside the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to build a proper plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work, and the government shouldn't panic. I'd say the same at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a good run as an accountant, maybe make manager, then switch before 2036. My job is mostly thinking work, so the robots coming in 2039 doesn't help me directly. But I could be running construction projects by then, which lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, buy the house, start a family, and keep using the AI tools as they become normal. Around 2030 I'd start moving into construction project work, maybe with a part-time course. I'd save hard so Grace could go part-time when the children are small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's long enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands and keep their faith, and to use the AI without depending on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you worry less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, quite a lot less. I'd still think about it, but it wouldn't stop us having a family. That's the main thing.

say: I'd call ten years **plenty** for anyone willing to work.
I'd say the **government** shouldn't panic or try to run everything.
think: I'd have a good run, maybe **manager**, then **switch** before 2036.
The **robot delay** doesn't help my thinking work directly.
do: Start moving into **construction project** work around **2030**.
Save so my wife can go **part-time** with small children.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands and keep their faith, and to use the AI without depending on it.
fieldNote: He still expects to **switch careers**, so anxious, though he sounds hopeful.
Ten years means he won't **delay** a family.
He applies a **hands-and-faith** philosophy to his future children.

steps.text: Buy the house and start a family
Move into construction project work around 2030
Save so his wife can work part-time with small children
Use the AI tools as they become normal at the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits before we've got a house or children. What would help is apprenticeships and on-the-job training for people switching into trades, and help for small firms to take them on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith and family. Everybody talks about jobs, but for me the question is whether I can provide for my family, whatever happens. A man wants to know he can keep a roof over his family.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about jobs, but for me the question is whether I can provide for my family, whatever happens.
portrait: Emeka is a **junior accountant** at a sixty-person firm that serves construction businesses.
He's married to a pharmacist, has strong **savings**, and plans a house and **children**.
He uses AI **now and then**, after his team proves it, and is weak on spotting hidden expenses.
He moves from calm to **alarmed**, blaming no one and taking **personal responsibility**.
His plan is to move into **construction site management** through his clients.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and on-the-job training for people **switching trades**.
